title: A task whose claim response is lost stays 'assigned' forever while the node keeps polling. Cancel cannot clear it and the federated round stalls.
scenario:
1. The iPad has a 25 s long-poll open on GET /nodes/ipad-x/next.
2. The user backgrounds the app or turns 'Serve tasks' off. NodeService.stop() cancels the loop task (NodeService.swift:110-115, 81-88), and URLSession cancels the request. The server thread never notices and keeps waiting in cond.wait.
3. A train_lora round task targeted at this iPad, or any generate task, is created inside that window. The dead poll claims it: attempts=1, status=assigned, assigned_to=ipad-x. The response goes to a closed socket.
4. The app returns within 75 s, or within 25 s, when the dead poll and the new live poll both wait and race for the same notify_all. The new loop heartbeats and polls.
5. _claim only returns tasks with status=='queued', so the node never gets the task back. sweep() only requeues tasks whose node is offline, and this node is online. The task stays 'assigned' indefinitely.
6. POST /tasks/{id}/cancel only sets cancel_requested, which a node only sees on its next event POST, and none ever comes. The task can't be cancelled either.
7. Federation._maybe_aggregate waits for every round task to be terminal (federated.py:210), so the round stays 'running' forever.
The same orphan happens when the client's POST /complete fails once. The client never retries it (NodeService.swift:214-226: the error only goes to lastError), and the task stays 'running' on an online node.
Reproduced against the origin/fleet sources copied to a temp dir: claim with next_task(node, 0), drop the result, then call next_task three more times plus sweep(). Result: 're-poll returns None ; task status assigned assigned_to ipad-aaaa1111'.
evidence:
fleet.py:187 `if m["status"] == "queued" and m["kind"] in kinds and m["target"] in (None, node_id): return t` (an already-assigned task is never re-delivered).
fleet.py:135-137 sweep only considers `not self._online(self.nodes.get(t.meta.get("assigned_to") ...))`.
next_task refreshes last_seen on every poll (fleet.py:198), so the owning node never looks offline.
NodeService.swift:214-221: complete runs once in a detached Task with no retry. On failure: `if let reported { lastError = "Couldn't report ..." }`.
fix: Server: in next_task, before claiming new work, re-deliver any task with status 'assigned' and assigned_to==node_id, without incrementing attempts. Treat a poll from a node that still owns a 'running' task as abandonment and pass that task to _requeue_or_lose, since a node runs one task at a time. Client: retry complete() with backoff until it gets a 2xx, 404 or 409.

title: next_task flips the status to 'assigned' outside fleet.cond, so concurrent polls can claim the same task (double claim). Cancel and sweep have the same check-then-act race.
scenario:
1. Several nodes are long-polling.
2. A generate task is created with no target. MCP run_on_node without `node` does this (mcp_bridge.py t_run_on_node).
3. notify_all wakes every waiter. Waiter A runs _claim under fleet.cond, increments attempts, releases cond, and only then calls task.set_status('assigned').
4. Waiter B gets cond in that gap. _claim still sees status=='queued', so B claims the same task.
5. Both nodes receive the task and run the prompt. assigned_to is whichever set_status ran last, and attempts=2 after a single real assignment. The losing node's current_task stays stale. The next time the winner goes offline, _requeue_or_lose sees attempts>=max_attempts and marks the task 'lost' instead of retrying it.
Reproduced with 6 waiting nodes and sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6): 2 of 40 trials double-claimed, e.g. 'handed to [ipad-0001aaaa, ipad-0004aaaa] attempts 2 assigned_to ipad-0004aaaa'.
The same unlocked pattern lets cancel() (status read without fleet.cond, line 282) finish a 'queued' task as 'cancelled' and fire the round listener. The concurrent claim's set_status('assigned') then overwrites the terminal status, and the task runs anyway.
sweep() acts on a snapshot taken under cond (lines 134-142) without re-checking. It can requeue a task that complete() just finished, or mark 'lost' a task another node reclaimed in between.
evidence:
fleet.py:196-208:
```
with self.cond:
    while True: ... task = self._claim(node_id) ...
    task.meta["attempts"] = ...+1
    self.nodes[node_id]["current_task"] = task.id
task.set_status("assigned", assigned_to=node_id)   # outside the lock
```
fleet.py:282-284 `status = task.meta["status"]; if status == "queued": self._finish(task, "cancelled", ...)` runs without fleet.cond.
fleet.py:138-142 calls `_requeue_or_lose` on the stale snapshot.
fix: In next_task, set meta status='assigned' and assigned_to inside the same `with self.cond` block as _claim, then persist. Under fleet.cond, re-check the current status in cancel(), _requeue_or_lose() and complete()/_finish before transitioning, and never overwrite a terminal status.

It then leaves the `with self.cond` block. Only after that, at line 208, does it call task.set_status('assigned', ...). In jobworker.Job, set_status takes task.cond, which is a separate lock (Job.cond = threading.Condition(self.lock)), so nothing serializes it with fleet.cond. _claim (lines 182-189) picks any task whose meta status is 'queued'. The server is a ThreadingHTTPServer with daemon_threads, so long-polls really do run on concurrent threads. create_task's notify_all wakes every waiter. The second waiter to get fleet.cond still sees 'queued' and claims the same task.

The race window is wider than a GIL switch. set_status runs save_meta, a file write plus os.replace, and then append, which does an fsync. All of that file I/O releases the GIL before the status change is visible.

I ran a deterministic repro in a temp dir outside the repo, using copies of fleet.py and jobworker.py from origin/fleet. I wrapped set_status('assigned') with a 50 ms delay and had 3 heartbeated nodes long-polling. One untargeted generate task then went to all 3 nodes, with attempts=3 and assigned_to=node-2, the last writer. That confirms the double claim and the inflated attempts count. With attempts at or above max_attempts (2), _requeue_or_lose sends the task to 'lost' on the next offline sweep instead of retrying it.

The persist and append steps (save_meta and the 'status' event) can then run after releasing the lock, or under task.cond. Because _claim only selects 'queued' tasks, an in-memory flip under fleet.cond is enough to exclude other waiters. In cancel(), _requeue_or_lose() and _finish(), take fleet.cond and re-read the current status before transitioning. Skip the transition if the task is already terminal. In sweep, also re-check that the task is still assigned/running to the same assigned_to that was seen in the snapshot. Treat 'succeeded', 'failed', 'cancelled' and 'lost' as absorbing states that set_status callers in fleet must never overwrite.

The effects are duplicate compute, wrong attempt accounting that leads to premature 'lost', and a cancelled task resurrected after its round listener fired. | fix: In next_task, keep the status transition inside the same `with self.cond` block as _claim: set task.meta status='assigned', assigned_to=node_id, updated_at and attempts there and call save_meta, then call task.append('status', ...) after releasing the lock. In cancel(), _requeue_or_lose(), sweep() and complete()/_finish, take fleet.cond, re-read the current status and assigned_to, and skip the transition if the task has become terminal or has been reassigned since the snapshot. title: The worker crashes on startup when an in-flight task has used up its attempts: _finish runs before self._listeners exists.
scenario:
1. A task was requeued once, for example because the iPad was backgrounded for more than 75 s, and then reclaimed, so attempts=2.
2. The worker process restarts while that task is 'assigned' or 'running'.
3. Fleet.__init__ calls self._load(). _load calls _requeue_or_lose, which sees attempts>=2 and calls _finish(task, 'lost').
4. _finish iterates self._listeners, which is only assigned on the next line. The result is AttributeError and the jobworker exits during make_router.
The 'lost' status was persisted before the exception, so each restart clears one such task. Every task in that state costs one crash.
Reproduced: 'restart CRASH: AttributeError 'Fleet' object has no attribute '_listeners'', followed by 'second restart OK; status now lost'.
evidence:
fleet.py:56-57
```
self._load()
self._listeners: list = []  # callables(task_meta) on terminal
```
fleet.py:71-72 `_load` calls `self._requeue_or_lose(task, "worker restarted")`.
fleet.py:96-99 calls `_finish` when attempts >= max_attempts.
fleet.py:89 `for fn in self._listeners:`.

If they need to, collect those tasks during _load and notify the listeners after registration, or have the listener re-scan terminal tasks.

title: Remotely triggered LoRA training on the user's private documents is on by default, needs no consent on the device, and the resulting per-device adapter can be downloaded by any token holder
scenario: A caller sends start_fed_round with only base_model and no examples. This can be a prompt-injected Claude on the Funnel bridge, or any holder of the worker token posting to POST /fed/rounds or POST /tasks. The worker sets use_local_data=True because it defaults to `not examples` (PoC printed `use_local_data = True`). The iPad runs the task with no prompt or setting. It cuts every imported document into up to 400 samples (`samples += await localSamples()`) and trains with up to 5000 iterations at lr up to 0.1, rank 64. It then uploads adapter.safetensors. Any token holder can fetch that raw, un-averaged adapter with GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/adapter.safetensors. An adapter fit that hard to a few hundred chunks memorizes them, so the document text can be regenerated. This contradicts the README claim 'Raw data never leaves the device'. The only switch on the device is 'Serve tasks', and nothing there mentions documents.
evidence: federated.py:171 `use_local = bool(spec.get("use_local_data", not examples))`; fleet.py:344-348 serves `GET /tasks/{id}/artifacts/{name}` to any bearer; NodeService.swift:368 (origin/ios-node) `if p.useLocalData ?? false { samples += await localSamples() }` with no user check; NodeSettingsSection.swift footer only says 'Pulls generate and LoRA training tasks'. README (origin/fleet): 'Raw data never leaves the device.'
fix: Default use_local_data to False. Add an opt-in on the device ('Allow training on my imported documents', off by default) and check it in runTrain; fail the task when it is off. Do not serve per-node adapters over GET; only the coordinator should read them, and only the FedAvg result should be published. Expose the document-training flag in the MCP description so Claude must ask the user.

title: Artifact upload reads the whole body into RAM before checking ownership, a negative Content-Length bypasses the 300 MB cap, and F16 aggregation inflates memory about 20x
scenario: A token holder sends PUT /tasks/<any id>/artifacts/x with `Content-Length: -1` and streams data. `n > limit` is False for negative n, so `rfile.read(-1)` reads until EOF into one bytes object, with no limit and no socket timeout on the worker Handler. PoC with the cap shrunk to 1000 bytes: honest CL=5000 gave 'body too large', while CL=-1 with the same 5000 bytes was accepted as `{"bytes": 5000}`. Ownership and MAX_ARTIFACT are checked only after the read, so concurrent 300 MB PUTs each hold 300 MB even for tasks the sender does not own. Separately, a node that completes with a 256 MB F16 adapter makes read_safetensors build a tuple of Python floats via struct.unpack. Measured: a 16 MB F16 file reached a 305 MiB peak (20x) and took 7.8 s, so 256 MB means about 5 GB and minutes of work. That runs under fed.lock inside the node's /complete request, longer than the iPad's 45 s request timeout.
evidence: jobworker.py:415-419 `n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0); if n > limit: raise ...; return self.rfile.read(n) if n else b""`; fleet.py:346 `fleet.put_artifact(tid, q.get("node_id", ""), sub[1], raw_reader())` (body is read before `_owned`); federated.py:50 `array("f", struct.unpack(f"<{len(buf) // 2}e", buf))`; aggregation runs synchronously from Fleet._finish listeners (fleet.py:89-91).
fix: Reject n < 0 in _raw and _body. Check ownership and the name before reading, and stream the body to the .part file in chunks while enforcing MAX_ARTIFACT. Set Handler.timeout. Decode F16 with `array('f', memoryview(buf).cast('e'))` and run aggregation in a background thread instead of the /complete request.

title: start_fed_round and train_lora payloads have no enforced size or hyperparameter limits, so a remote caller can crash or tie up the iPad
